newsitem.title: USA: Northeast to battle "weak sister" image in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Northeast to battle "weak sister" image in 1997.

text.p: The Northeast will try to shed its status as a high-cost business region riddled with out-moded, shrinking industries, but, economists said, it will likely remain an economic laggard.
Rae Rosen, senior economist at the New York Federal Reserve Bank, forecast 1997 employment growth at a 1 percent rate for the tri-state region of New York, New Jersey and Connecticut.
"We are getting reasonably good jobs growth for a mature area of the country, but we're still one of the slowest regions, if not the slowest," she said.

The prospects for New England, which stretches from Maine to Connecticut, are brighter than those for the Middle Atlantic states, which encompass New York to Pennsylvania, said Ross DeVol, senior vice president at WEFA Group, an economic consulting firm in Philadelphia.

He predicted the number of jobs will grow 1.3 percent in New England this year, more than the foreseen 0.8 percent rise in the Mid-Atlantic states, but less than the expected national average of 2.0 percent.

A recent rash of government lay-offs and job-cutting corporate restructurings within many key industries in the Northeast -- including defence, healthcare, insurance and banking -- should decline in 1997, lifting the region's prospects, analysts said.

"When I look out to '97, what I see happening is what I call convergence -- many of the Northeast states' economies start to look more like each other and more like the United States," said Nicholas Perna, chief economist of Fleet Financial Group, which operates in the Northeast.
Also, recent tax cuts in some states within the area should spur investment, along with efforts to reduce the region's relatively high cost of energy and manufacturing wages.

"We've seen some efforts to reduce taxes in New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Massachusetts. Longer-term, these cuts will help the region, but in the short-term they will not be a magic fix," DeVol said.
Perhaps the greatest hope lies in a growing presence of dynamic industries new to the Northeast which could serve as an engine for growth in 1997 and beyond.
In New York City alone, 8,000 new jobs were created by the burgeoning film industry in 1996, a number the Fed's Rosen called "astounding".

The creation of new entertainment/media monoliths such as Walt Disney Co., which purchased Capital Cities/ABC Inc. last year for $19 billion, could draw even more Hollywood dollars to New York, analysts said.

Boston is experiencing explosive growth in the bio-technology industry, while Wall Street has just enjoyed a banner year and market pundits are not calling for massive lay-offs when, and if, the markets' fantastic bull run falters.
"Wall Street was remarkably restrained this time around on the hiring and we didn't get that type of employment-binge seen in the last boom in the late 80s," Rosen said.
The soaring popularity of mutual funds should continue to fuel growth in Massachusetts, the home of such industry powerhouses as Fidelity Investments and Putnam Investments.

Also, Boston's so-called Silicon Valley of the East has recently staged a minor come-back. Internet- and intranet-related firms have revitalised the area, which was hard hit in years past after local mainframe computer firms lost a competitive battle with the network personal computer businesses in the West, analysts said.
Cutting-edge industries such as photonics -- the use of light lasers and fiber optics to send and receive data -- are starting to shun the West Coast and call the Northeast home, economists said.
